title: Guides for prayer (CCC 2685–2690)
hookLine: families, clergy, religious, prayer groups, spiritual directors

cards: Jesus has just finished praying, off to the side, and his disciples have been watching. They've seen the healings, heard the parables. And when he comes back, what one of them asks for isn't a miracle or an explanation.
It's a lesson. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." The ones closest to him, who have seen all of it, still ask to be taught.
So who does that teaching now? Today: guides for prayer.

teach.b: The Catechism's answer begins at home. It calls the Christian family the first place prayer is learned, and gives that home a name: the domestic church.
A grace before supper, a sign of the cross on a sleeping child's forehead, a parent kneeling by a bed: that's where a child first sees what praying looks like.
Paul writes to Timothy of a faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, before it lived in him.
Then the Church's ministers. Priests and deacons, the Catechism says, are responsible for forming people in prayer, not only leading it.
Next, people in religious life, monks, nuns, sisters and brothers, many of whom have given their lives to prayer; their monasteries and convents keep a rhythm others can join or learn from.
Then prayer groups, which the Catechism calls schools of prayer: a few people around a table, a Bible open, a rosary passed around a parish hall.
And last, spiritual direction. Some Catholics meet regularly with one wise person, a priest, a sister or a trained lay guide, to talk honestly about their prayer.
Drawing on John of the Cross, the Catechism says the choice matters: a guide should be learned, prudent and experienced. Nobody is expected to work prayer out alone in a locked room.
Even the disciples, standing next to Jesus, asked.

how: Catholics usually first learn prayer at home, then through parish catechesis, prayer groups and retreats; some meet regularly with a spiritual director to talk about their prayer life.

games.q: you're one of the disciples. you've watched Jesus heal and teach. he comes back from praying. what do you ask him for?
games.why: "Lord, teach us to pray." the ones closest to him still asked for a lesson, and Jesus answered with the Our Father.

practice: Bring to mind one person who showed you how to pray, or how to be still, or how to hope: a grandparent, a teacher, a stranger in a pew. Then think of one person who could teach you a little more.
If you pray, thank God for the first and ask for courage with the second; if you don't, simply hold them both in mind.
